children: The worst-case scenario is that AI could disappoint - causing stocks to fall and damaging the economy
Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh was part of an event in San Francisco on Monday that looked at the role of AI in the economy.

The Federal Reserve staff is in the early days of developing various scenarios of how artificial intelligence's growing role in business and daily life will impact the economy, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said Monday.

"Our responsibility is to recognize that the widespread adoption of this technology will have significant impact on the economy, with important implications for monetary policy down the road," Warsh said at the start of an all-day forum, held at the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco, on how AI will impact the labor market.
Warsh laid out three scenarios that he said were the starting point for the discussions.
At one end is the most favorable outcome, where AI leads to an increase in productivity and "economic gains are shared broadly across labor and the owners of capital," he said.

Other outcomes were less positive, including one where there is substantial loss of jobs. The worst-case scenario, he said, is one where AI turns out to be less transformative than promised - leading to stock-market weakness followed by an economic slowdown and a rise in unemployment.
"These are illustrative scenarios, not forecasts," and are just designed to get the conversation started, Warsh noted.

"My Fed colleagues and I are not at this conference as futurists. ... Our job is to prepare for whatever comes next," Warsh said. "Many other outcomes - probably including one that will prove most accurate - could be drawn."

The conference on AI and labor is part of the efforts of a Fed task force created to look at the issue. It's one of five task forces Warsh set up when he took the helm of the central bank earlier this year to review how the Fed is tackling important topics.
The AI group asked Warsh to hold a public discussion across a wide section of industry and academia.
In his speech, Warsh didn't address the Fed-related topic on many investors' minds: How the central bank might respond to the hot October consumer-price inflation report released last week.
Fed governor Christopher Waller caused short-term market yields to spike last Tuesday by saying he would support a 50-basis-point interest-rate hike at the next policy meeting in early December.
Does Waller have company for upsizing?

Derek Holt, chief economist at Scotia Bank, said we will likely never know what Warsh thinks about rate policy because he prefers not to preview his views. Based on his reading of other Fed speeches, Holt said he thinks that Waller "is on his own" in terms of a possible half-point move.
In his speech, Warsh did not repeat his earlier views about how AI technology might lower inflation. Holt said that Warsh had already begun to distance himself from this "dovish" view.
